REM vs EM: what changes, and why

Rem follows the root font size. Em follows an element’s font size, with a different reference when you set font-size itself. That distinction explains most surprising conversions.

By ParseCove · Published 27 November 2026

On this pageThe differenceTry the numbersNested em valuesChoose a unitTermsFAQ

REM vs EM vs PX: the reference is the difference

For a regular element’s font-size, an em value multiplies the inherited font size. For padding, it multiplies that element’s own computed font size. A rem value on these properties uses the root font size, normally that of <html>. A px value is a CSS pixel length.

Reference used by ordinary element declarations
DeclarationWhat 1 unit refers toAt root 16px, parent 20px, child 25px
font-size: 1emInherited font size20px
padding: 1emThe element’s own font size25px
padding: 1remRoot font size16px
padding: 16px16 CSS pixels16px

Reference: MDN: CSS lengths. Root font-size and media-query contexts have additional rules; see the FAQ below.

html { font-size: 16px; }

The controls model a separate page. The parent’s px size stays independent of the root. Bars compare lengths on the same relative scale. Outputs are rounded to four decimal places.

Why nested em font sizes compound

Suppose a container has a 16px font and two nested elements each declare font-size: 1.25em. The first becomes 20px. The second uses that inherited 20px and becomes 25px. A third level would be 31.25px. Each declaration introduces another multiplication.

A complete nested example

<style>
  .base { font-size: 16px; }
  .level { font-size: 1.25em; }
</style>
<div class="base">
  <div class="level">20px
    <div class="level">25px</div>
  </div>
</div>

With font-size: 1.25rem instead, both nested elements resolve to 20px when the root is 16px. Changing the parent’s font size does not add another rem multiplication. Merely nesting elements does not compound font size: the repeated relative declaration causes it.

Reference: MDN: font-size and nested em values.

When should you use rem, em or px?

Choose the reference that matches the relationship you want. A component can reasonably use all three units.

GoalA useful starting pointReason
A page-wide typography or spacing scaleremOne root reference keeps unrelated components on the same scale.
A button’s padding that follows its textemThe padding can grow when that button’s own font grows.
A border with a fixed CSS pixel widthpxThe width stays independent of the font-size reference.
Line height that follows inherited text sizesA unitless numberA multiplier such as 1.5 inherits as a number rather than a computed length.

A component using the three relationships

html { font-size: 100%; }
.card {
  font-size: 1.125rem;
  padding: 1em;
  border: 1px solid #d9e1ef;
  line-height: 1.5;
}
.card__title { font-size: 1.25em; }

At a computed 16px root, this card has an 18px font and 18px padding. Its title is 22.5px. At a 20px root those values become 22.5px, 22.5px and 28.125px. The border stays 1 CSS pixel. 100% does not guarantee 16px; the browser’s initial font size and the user’s settings still matter.

Test the component with larger default text, page zoom and narrow viewports. Using rem or em alone does not guarantee accessible text or a layout that reflows well. CSS pixels can also scale with page zoom; a CSS pixel is not necessarily one physical display pixel.

References: MDN: unitless line-height · W3C CSS Values: absolute lengths.

Terms used in this guide

Root element
The top element of an HTML document, normally <html>. Its font size supplies the rem reference for ordinary element declarations.
Computed font size
The font size after CSS rules and relative references have been resolved. Browser developer tools expose the computed value in CSS pixels.
Inherited font size
The font size passed down from an element’s parent. An em value on the element’s own font-size uses this starting size.
CSS pixel
A reference length used by CSS. Its relationship to physical display pixels depends on the display and browser settings.
Compounding
Repeated multiplication when nested elements each set a relative font size. In the worked example, 16 × 1.25 × 1.25 produces 25px.

Common questions

Is 1rem always 16px?

No. For the ordinary element declarations shown here, 1rem equals the computed root font size. Check your page rather than assuming the browser default. Use the REM to PX converter with that root size for a numeric result.

Does em always use the parent’s font size?

No. On font-size it uses the inherited font size; on properties such as padding it uses the element’s own computed font size. That is why the live example has different em results for font-size and padding.

What happens on the root’s own font-size?

A rem value on the root’s own font-size refers to the initial font size, so it does not depend circularly on the root size being calculated. The live comparison models declarations on regular child elements.

Do media queries use the same font references?

Font-relative units used outside an element context, such as media queries, use initial font metrics. Do not calculate a media-query breakpoint from a component’s current font size. Check the W3C font-relative length rules for this separate context.

Should I replace every px value with rem?

No blanket replacement is needed. Decide whether the value should follow root text, local text or a fixed CSS pixel length. Then test the result with zoom, larger text and the layouts you support.

Reference for root and media-query contexts: W3C CSS Values and Units Level 4, font-relative lengths (Working Draft).
